strengths: Hardware and Dataset Initiative: Developing the custom 'NeuroBuds' earphone prototype and gathering free-living ExG alongside multi-sensory task data (DailySense) represents a substantial data collection and engineering effort.

Physiological Motivation: Decomposing ExG into 12 physiologically canonical bands (EEG, EMG, EOG, ECG) provides an intuitive domain-informed inductive bias compared to generic single-channel wideband processing.

Practical Deployment Considerations: The inclusion of on-device runtime analysis on a mobile phone (inference latency, memory footprint) demonstrates practical awareness of wearable deployment constraints.
weaknesses: Severe Evaluation Flaw (Data Leakage via Random Window Shuffling): In both Section 5.1 and Appendix F, the authors state that continuous time-series data were segmented into 4-second windows and randomly shuffled into 80/20 train/test splits within subjects. In continuous physiological recordings, adjacent windows share strong temporal autocorrelation, background brain states, electrode impedance drift, and environmental noise. This leads to artificial performance inflation. The severity of this leakage is confirmed in Table 7 (Appendix L), where performance collapses under cross-subject evaluation (average F1 drops from 0.876 to 0.586), and PiMT's gaze tracking error worsens to 7.78°, performing worse than baseline PatchTST (7.07°).

Flawed Public Benchmark Protocol: The public benchmarks (SEED, DREAMER, Sleep-EDF, BCI Competition IV 2b) were also evaluated using random 80/20 window-shuffled splits rather than standard subject-independent (LOSO) or trial-independent splits established in the literature. Consequently, the reported results in Table 2 cannot be meaningfully compared to existing literature, and only two baselines (PatchTST and Bidirectional-Mamba) trained under the same flawed split are reported.

Limited Methodological Novelty: Methodologically, the approach consists of applying a classical 12-channel bandpass filter bank (a standard technique in BCI for decades, e.g., Filter Bank CSP), linearly projecting time patches, feeding them into an off-the-shelf Bidirectional-Mamba backbone, and optimizing a linear combination of standard MAE reconstruction losses (autoencoding and masked time/frequency reconstruction). The machine learning contributions are incremental.

Overstated 'Foundation Model' Claims: The manuscript repeatedly frames the method and data as an ExG foundation model. However, pretraining on only 50 hours of ExG from 22 participants falls drastically short of true foundation model scale, especially compared to recent biosignal models trained on thousands of subjects and tens of thousands of hours.

Confounding Artifacts in Downstream Sensory Tasks: The sensory tasks rely on very small participant cohorts (up to 7 participants per task) and binary contrasts that easily introduce severe muscle (EMG) or eye (EOG) artifacts (e.g., tasting vinegar vs. chocolate milk induces grimacing/swallowing; comedy vs. documentary induces smiling/laughter). It remains unverified whether the model is decoding true neural sensory processing or merely trivial facial/ocular artifact signatures.

strengths: Holistic system design spanning custom unobtrusive hardware (NeuroBuds earhook prototype), a dedicated multi-sensory dataset (DailySense), and a tailored representation learning architecture.

The concept of Physiology-informed Multi-band Tokenization (PiMT) is well-motivated by domain knowledge, providing an intuitive and structured way to handle the wide spectral differences across ExG modalities (EEG, EOG, EMG, ECG).

Comprehensive ablation study covering frequency band decomposition granularities (1, 2, 4, 12 bands), pre-training loss components (time- vs. frequency-domain reconstructions), patch sizes, and backbone choices (Mamba vs. Transformer).
On-device mobile benchmarking demonstrating feasibility of real-time inference on edge devices (Samsung Galaxy S24).
weaknesses: Flawed evaluation split strategy in main experiments: The main results (Table 1) use random window-level shuffling (splitting 4-second non-overlapping windows into 80/20 train/test). In continuous biosignals, adjacent temporal windows share substantial autocorrelation and noise profiles, causing severe temporal data leakage. When evaluated in true cross-subject or cross-session settings (Appendix L, Table 7), performance drops precipitously (e.g., average classification F1 drops from 87.6% to 58.6% across mostly binary tasks). Cross-session or cross-subject splits should be the primary evaluation metric.

Misleading presentation of cross-participant generalization: Figure 7 claims to show Leave-One-Subject-Out (LOSO) results, but the text clarifies that the target subject is only excluded from pre-training, while task fine-tuning still includes target subject data. Given that Table 7 reports true cross-subject performance at 58.6%, presenting Figure 7 as generalization to unseen users is confusing and potentially misleading.

Incomplete benchmarking and missing details on public datasets: Table 2 evaluates only against PatchTST and Bidirectional-Mamba, omitting ExG-specific foundation models and architectures (e.g., BIOT, LaBraM, EEGNet, EEGConformer). Additionally, it is unclear whether the public benchmark models were fine-tuned from DailySense pre-training or pre-trained/trained from scratch, especially given disparate channel layouts (e.g., 62 channels for SEED vs. 2 channels for Sleep-EDF).

Inconsistencies and technical clarity: Section 4 states there are 50 hours of free-living unlabeled data, whereas Appendix G states pre-training was done on 'the entire 40 hours of free-living data'. Figure 1 caption introduces 'PiFT' while the text uses 'PiMT'.

strengths: End-to-end system contribution: The authors developed custom hardware (NeuroBuds), an 8-channel earphone-based ExG device capable of unobtrusively capturing near-ear EEG, EOG, and EMG in daily living conditions.

Novel and diverse benchmark dataset (DailySense): Curating 50 hours of free-living continuous ExG data alongside 20 hours of task-specific recordings spanning all five human senses is a valuable and refreshing contribution to the wearable physiological sensing domain.

Physiology-informed tokenization: Decomposing broad-spectrum ExG into 12 physiologically grounded sub-bands (PiMT) effectively addresses the classic trade-off between broad-band noise susceptibility and narrow-band task specificity.

Extensive experimental validation: Beyond DailySense (spanning six distinct tasks), the method is benchmarked across four standard public datasets (DREAMER, SEED, Sleep-EDF, and BCI Comp IV 2b) against strong contemporary baselines (PatchTST, Bidirectional-Mamba, EEGConformer), consistently achieving superior performance.

Thorough auxiliary analyses: The paper provides meaningful frequency saliency visualizations, pre-training scaling trends, ablation studies across reconstruction objectives and patch lengths, and mobile on-device latency profiling.
weaknesses: Evaluation protocol and potential data leakage in the main results: As described in Appendix F, data segmentation splits 4-second windows via a random 80/20 shuffle. In continuous time-series, randomly splitting consecutive windows from the same recording session introduces temporal autocorrelation and label leakage between adjacent windows. This likely explains why main table scores are very high (F1 > 0.96 for video/audio) but drop markedly under the cross-subject (F1 ~ 0.58) and cross-session (F1 ~ 0.70) splits in Appendix L (Table 7). The cross-session/cross-subject evaluations reflect real-world utility more faithfully and should ideally be highlighted in the main text.

Ambiguity in 'LOSO' terminology in Section 5.6: The Leave-One-Subject-Out experiment in Section 5.6 (Figure 7) actually refers to excluding the subject only from self-supervised pre-training, after which downstream fine-tuning still uses the subject's labeled data. In biomedical ML literature, 'LOSO' conventionally denotes cross-subject transfer where the evaluation subject is completely held out from downstream supervised training. Clarifying this distinction in the text would prevent confusion with the cross-subject results in Table 7.

Spectral redundancy in filter bank: Several defined sub-bands overlap substantially (e.g., EOG-overall [0.1–20 Hz] heavily overlaps with EEG delta, theta, alpha, and ECG LF/HF bands; QRS complex [8–50 Hz] overlaps with alpha, beta, and EMG-LF). The paper does not thoroughly discuss or ablate the impact of this spectral redundancy or the potential phase distortion introduced by multi-band IIR/FIR filtering compared to non-overlapping band partitioning.

Early performance saturation: As shown in Figure 6, downstream classification performance plateaus at around 30% (~15 hours) of pre-training data. Given that foundation model paradigms emphasize power-law scaling with increasing pre-training volume, the authors should discuss whether this saturation stems from limited subject diversity (22 participants) or architectural capacity constraints.

strengths: Holistic hardware-algorithm co-design: The paper provides a complete pipeline from custom low-cost earphone hardware prototyping (NeuroBuds, $80) and data curation (DailySense: 50 hours free-living, 20 hours across five senses) to representation learning.

Physiologically grounded tokenization: Rather than relying on rigid task-specific filtering or naive wide-band inputs, Physiology-informed Multi-band Tokenization (PiMT) effectively decomposes signals into 12 canonical ExG sub-bands, preserving both temporal and spectral cues.

Extensive experimental evaluation: The proposed method is thoroughly evaluated on both the new DailySense benchmark and four standard public EEG/ExG benchmarks (SEED, DREAMER, Sleep-EDF, BCI-IV 2b), demonstrating consistent improvements over competitive baselines including PatchTST and Bidirectional-Mamba.

Detailed ablation and practical validation: The manuscript provides thorough analyses, including tokenization granularity ablations, saliency maps, pre-training loss ablations, hardware correlation against research-grade OpenBCI, and on-device smartphone latency profiling.
weaknesses: Methodological flaw in main data splitting (temporal leakage): In Section 5.1 and Appendix F, the evaluation protocol segments continuous recordings into 4-second windows and randomly shuffles them before taking an 80/20 train/test split. In continuous physiological and sensory signals, adjacent windows have strong temporal autocorrelation, which significantly inflates reported within-session scores (0.876 average F1) compared to more realistic cross-session (0.700) or cross-subject (0.586) evaluations shown in Table 12.

Limited dataset cohort scale: Although curating free-living data is challenging, 50 hours from 22 subjects for pre-training and only 6–7 subjects per downstream task is relatively modest for training and validating a general-purpose 'foundation model'.

Dataset and hardware accessibility: The dataset DailySense is currently not guaranteed to be publicly released (noted as pending legal review in Footnote 1), and because NeuroBuds is a custom hardware prototype, verifying reproducibility for the ear-ExG sensory tasks will be difficult for the broader community.

Sequence length explosion: Decomposing each channel into 12 sub-bands multiplies the effective sequence length fed into the encoder by 12x, which increases memory and compute requirements despite using linear-complexity state-space models.

strengths: Holistic hardware-data-algorithm co-design: The authors integrate a custom wearable earphone prototype (NeuroBuds), a novel free-living ExG dataset (DailySense) covering five human senses, and a specialized modeling framework.

Physiologically grounded tokenization (PiMT): Decomposing ExG signals into 12 canonical physiological frequency bands provides an intuitive and effective inductive bias for learning task-agnostic ExG representations without requiring manual frequency selection per downstream task.

Extensive experimental validation: The paper evaluates the proposed method across six diverse sensory tasks on DailySense as well as four widely recognized public ExG benchmarks (SEED, DREAMER, Sleep-EDF, BCI Competition IV 2b), consistently outperforming strong baselines like PatchTST and Bidirectional-Mamba.

Thorough ablation and deployment studies: The authors provide detailed investigations into tokenization strategies, pre-training loss objectives, patch sizes, backbone choices (Mamba vs. Transformer), data scaling, leave-one-subject-out evaluation, and runtime feasibility on a commercial smartphone.
weaknesses: Potential data leakage in evaluation split: The primary evaluation on DailySense (and public benchmarks) uses a random 80/20 train/test split of shuffled 4-second windows (Section F). In physiological and continuous time-series signals, shuffling adjacent windows often leads to optimistic performance estimates due to temporal autocorrelation. While cross-session and cross-subject results are discussed in Appendix O (showing expected drops from 87.6% to 70.0% and 58.6%), relying on random window splits for the main benchmark tables is a methodological weakness.

Dataset accessibility: While the study is IRB-approved, the authors note in Footnote 1 that they are still working with legal counsel regarding dataset release. Lacking open access to the proprietary DailySense dataset restricts immediate reproducibility of the full sensing pipeline.

Computational redundancy of filter bank tokenization: Decomposing each channel into 12 parallel bands increases the token sequence length by a factor of 12. While Bidirectional-Mamba mitigates the quadratic scaling of standard Transformers, this still introduces noticeable memory and compute overhead relative to single-stream models.

strengths: Full-stack system effort: The authors present an end-to-end pipeline covering hardware prototyping (NeuroBuds earphone-based ExG sensing), dataset curation (DailySense with 50h free-living and 20h task-specific data), and model architecture.

Physiology-informed multi-band tokenization: Structuring multi-channel ExG signals into physiologically grounded canonical bands (EEG, EMG, EOG, ECG) provides an intuitive and structured representation that retains time-domain dynamics compared to standard STFT/CWT.

Comprehensive empirical analysis: The manuscript includes diverse downstream tasks across 6 tasks on DailySense and 4 public EEG benchmarks, accompanied by extensive ablation studies (patch size, backbone architecture, pre-training loss components, and filter-bank granularity).
On-device feasibility: The authors assess mobile inference latency (25 ms) and memory footprint on a modern smartphone, demonstrating the practical deployability of the representation pipeline.
weaknesses: Severe data leakage in evaluation protocol: For the primary benchmark results (Table 1), continuous recordings are segmented into 4-second windows and randomly shuffled into an 80/20 train/test split. In time-series and biosignal processing, randomly shuffling consecutive time windows from the same recording session causes heavy temporal autocorrelation leakage. In Appendix O (Table 12), when evaluated in a realistic cross-subject setting, the average F1-score collapses from 87.6% to 58.6% (near random chance for binary classification), demonstrating that the main reported metrics are heavily inflated.

Confounding physiological artifacts vs. true sensory neural decoding: The claim of decoding 'five human senses' from ear-ExG is overstated. Distinguishing sweet vs. sour liquid (chocolate milk vs. vinegar) or touch textures over 60 seconds is predominantly driven by peri-auricular EMG and movement artifacts (e.g., facial grimacing, swallowing, muscle tension) rather than cortical sensory representations, as hinted by the high-frequency band dominance in the saliency analysis.

Overstated 'foundation model' positioning on small cohort: Pre-training on 50 hours of unlabeled data from only 22 subjects—with downstream sensory tasks evaluated on only 6 to 7 subjects per task—does not substantiate claims of a generalizable 'ExG foundation model'. True biosignal foundation models typically leverage thousands of hours across hundreds or thousands of subjects.

Limited architectural novelty: Decomposing signals into standard clinical sub-bands via Butterworth bandpass filters is standard practice in EEG signal processing. Combining filter-bank outputs with linear patch tokenization and standard sequence models (Bidirectional Mamba) represents an incremental combination of existing techniques.

Incomplete benchmarking transparency: On the public datasets (Table 2), it is unclear whether the baselines (PatchTST, Bidirectional-Mamba) were trained from scratch or also pre-trained under comparable regimens, making it difficult to isolate the benefit of PiMT tokenization versus pre-training exposure.
